title: Stack Built on a Queue
statement:
Build a last-in, first-out stack of integers. The catch: the only storage you may use is one or two first-in, first-out queues, and you may only use queue operations on them: add to the back, take from the front, look at the front, size, and is-empty.

  • QueueStack() creates an empty stack.
  • push(x) puts x on top of the stack.
  • pop() removes the top value and returns it.
  • top() returns the top value without removing it.
  • empty() returns true if the stack holds nothing.

pop and top are only called on a non-empty stack.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the stack. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: 9 went in last, so it comes out first, even though a queue would hand back 4 first. The 4 is still there, so the stack is not empty.
Pops come out newest first: 3, then 2. The new 4 goes above the remaining 1.

constraints: pop and top are only called when the stack is not empty
hints: A queue hands values back oldest first; a stack needs newest first. Can you change the order inside the queue so the newest value sits at the front?
Right after adding x to the back, take every older value from the front and add it to the back again. How many values do you move?
Rotate size − 1 times after each push. Then the front of the queue is always the top of the stack, and pop and top are just queue front operations.

explain.intuition:
A queue is a line at a shop: people join at the back and leave from the front. A stack needs the person who joined last to leave first. You cannot reach the back of the line, but you can walk everyone in front of the newcomer around to the back of the line again.

So after each push, rotate the queue: take the front value and add it to the back, size − 1 times. The newcomer is now at the front, and the others keep their stack order behind it. Push costs O(n), and pop, top and empty become O(1). The other way round also works: keep pushes cheap and, on pop, move everything except the last value into a second queue.
steps: Keep a single queue q whose front is always the top of the stack.
push(x): add x to the back, then size − 1 times move the front value to the back.
pop(): take and return the front value.
top(): return the front value without removing it.
empty(): return whether the queue is empty.
pitfalls: Rotating size times instead of size − 1. That puts every value back where it was, and the newcomer ends up at the back again.
Using array tricks that are not queue operations, like reading the last element directly. The point of the exercise is to only touch the front and the back.

complexity.time: push O(n); pop, top, empty O(1)

solutions.title: Two queues, cheap push
solutions.idea: Push adds to the back of the main queue. Pop moves all but the last value into a helper queue, takes the last one, then swaps the queues. A separate field remembers the top for top().
solutions.time: push O(1), pop O(n), top O(1)

solutions.title: One queue, rotate on push
solutions.idea: After adding x, move the size − 1 older values from the front to the back, so x is at the front.
solutions.time: push O(n), pop O(1), top O(1)

followups: Do the reverse: build a queue from two stacks. Why does that one get amortized O(1) per operation while this one cannot?
Which of the two versions would you pick if pushes are rare and pops are frequent, and why?
